newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish truckers' strike ends after two weeks.
newsitem.headline: Spanish truckers' strike ends after two weeks.

text.p: Truckers in Spain said on Wednesday they had called off a strike lasting two weeks and affecting European industries, particularly carmakers, after meeting with government officials.

"It's been decided not to continue with the current work stoppage because of the economic consequences," Jose Maria Arambarri, a spokesman for the truckers' organisation leading the strike, told journalists. "There's been no type of deal."

The striking truckers reached the decision after a meeting with the government's director of land transport, Fernando Cascales, even though Fedatrans, the organisation leading the labour action, said there had been no overall accord.

"There didn't seem to be much sense in continuing to try to get pacts on concrete points," one of the truckers on the negotiating team said, adding that they were satisfied the problems in the transport sector were now widely understood.

The tension between strikers and the government in the two-week-long labour action had appeared to be easing earlier on Wednesday as police re-opened roads and the affected industries, particularly car-makers, had started to cope with the strike.
The government welcomed the decision and said it was still open to dialogue with the truckers.
"Their problems, even the biggest ones, are about to be solved in a permanent way through a process of dialogue with the sector," Spain's Development Minister Rafael Arias-Salgados told state media.
Strike pickets had stepped up their protest actions along Spanish highways earlier on Wednesday as talks to end the strike ended a marathon overnight session on a positive note.
There were still "situations of abnormality" in the Basque Country and the region of Cantabria, according to Industry Minister Josep Pique, who spoke earlier in parliament.

He said it was premature to assess the consequences of the strike in economic terms, but said that carmakers -- the worst hit by blocked roads and subsequent difficulties in getting supplies -- had restarted work earlier than anticipated.
Signs that the strike was near its end had been apparent in the optimism shown by some of the protesting truckers earlier on Wednesday.

Transporters in the central province of Burgos and on the Balearic Islands called off work stoppages, saying there had been progress. Taxi drivers, who are seeking the same kind of benefits as the truckers, decided to stop protest action pending talks.
Analysts in Spain had also expected a quick solution, based on government concessions.

"It does look like they will give in at least part of the way (to strikers' demands) and unfortunately this could have a trickle-down effect to other sectors," Heinrick Lumholdt, chief economist for Bank of America in Madrid, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

Petrol station owners threatened on Tuesday to stop pumping indefinitely if the government did not reconsider a planned liberalisation of the sector, which would allow truckers to buy fuel directly from wholesalers and bypass the filling stations.
This would cut back petrol stations' profit margins.
Carmakers struggled on Wednesday to restart production after police escorts helped unblock roads.

Volkswagen subsidiary SEAT began production at its Martorell plant after a two-day stoppage, but the German carmaker halted production of its Polo model at its main plant in Wolfsburg, Germany, which uses Spanish-made parts.
In Portugal, Opel also had to shut factories because of a dire parts' shortage due to the Spanish strike.
Food wholesalers were beginning to recover and Mercavalencia, the major wholesaler in Valencia, was offering all its normal supplies after several days of shortages.
A spokesman said trucks had been able to get through with police escorts and fresh produce and fish were arriving in good condition. The Agriculture Ministry said retail supplies were back to normal.
But divisions among the strikers emerged late on Tuesday as pickets opposed the return to work of some truckers and tried to block the freer flow of traffic.
